papers.title: Rational Ensemble Logic for Cohort Discovery with Real-World Electrophysiology Data
papers.abstract: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. On 54 manually constructed records, a prototype agreed with the assigned outcomes for base and strict post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries. A separate feasibility experiment over 1,976 patients identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds. The released prototype uses endpoint candidates and numerical tolerances. QEL supports the TRUER principle through explicit phenotype definitions, precise semantics, and provably correct evaluation procedures, with rational witnesses for existential queries. These provide a logical foundation for formal specification and correctness of algorithms that are independent of specific clinical interpretation, data annotation quality, and software implementation.

papers.title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
papers.abstract: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.

papers.title: Isabelle Pool Server: a pooled verification service for prover training and multi-agent proving
papers.abstract: Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a verification service with a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API, with session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, and a time budget on every call. Its verification interface spans single-step execution, block-level proof checking and whole-theory builds, with checkpoints for cheap branching and backtracking, and a build from scratch as the final arbiter. The service runs as a single container with monitoring and is accessible via a Python client, two MCP servers and a raw HTTP API. In our measurements IPS is level with PIDE MCP, a PIDE frontend for agents, at one worker and ahead of it at eight, at its commit of October 2026 (the tool is now PIDE AI). Once its sessions are up it scales to 32 concurrent workers on one host at 24 times the single-worker rate, and under memory pressure it refuses new sessions rather than losing existing ones. IPS is free software and publicly available at https://github.com/Deep-LCF/Isabelle-Pool-Server

papers.title: Finite model theory for pseudovarieties and universal algebra: preservation, definability and complexity
papers.abstract: We explore new interactions between finite model theory and classical streams of universal algebra and semigroup theory. A key result is an example of finite algebras whose variety is not finitely axiomatisable in first order logic, but where the class of finite members are finitely axiomatisable amongst finite algebras. These algebras present a negative solution to a first order formulation of the Eilenberg-Sch\"utzenberger problem, and witness the simultaneous failure of the {\L}os-Tarski Theorem, the SP-Preservation Theorem and Birkhoff's HSP-Preservation Theorem at the finite level. The examples also show that a pseudovariety without any finite pseudoequational basis may be finitely axiomatisable in first order logic amongst finite algebras. Other results include the undecidability of deciding first order definability of the pseudovariety of a finite algebra, and a mapping from any fixed finite template constraint satisfaction problem to a first order equivalent variety membership problem.

papers.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
papers.abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks normalization and makes algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($irrel : \Pi P{:}Prop.\,\Pi p,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, compile to unification-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$), and match declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) for open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

papers.title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
papers.abstract: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.

papers.title: Apply All, Prove Once: Embedding Parameterized Lemmas in DRAT
papers.abstract: The deletion-resolution-asymmetric-tautology (DRAT) proof format is widely used to express unsatisfiability proofs of Boolean formulas. Our DRATL format extends DRAT with parameterized lemmas, allowing a single proof to succinctly capture the common case where multiple instances of a pattern occur in a formula, differing in the identities and phases of the variables. Proofs expressed in DRATL can be hierarchical, with the proof of one lemma containing instantiations of others. Our elaborator program expands a DRATL proof containing multiple, nested lemmas into a standard DRAT proof. Most significantly, the elaboration yields compact proofs, where a single sequencing of the proof steps for each lemma covers all of its instantiations. Several case studies demonstrate that lemmas can provide a powerful method to generate short proofs for challenging problems.

papers.title: Matching-Logic-Based Understanding of Polynomial Functors and their Initial/Final Models Revisited
papers.abstract: Many data types used in programming are initial algebras or final coalgebras of polynomial functors. We show how to specify them uniformly in matching logic, using the representation of polynomial functors as unary container functors $X\mapsto\sum_{a:A}X^{B[a]}$. For each container functor, we give a matching logic theory of its initial algebra and one of its final coalgebra. Besides the no-junk and no-confusion axioms and their duals, these theories include axioms about the elements that represent functions, for the initial algebra, and a bisimilarity axiom and a realisation axiom, for the final coalgebra; the existence axioms use free set variables to range over all subsets of a model. We prove that, in every model, the algebra extracted from the model is an initial algebra (a W-type) and the extracted coalgebra is a final coalgebra (an M-type) of the container extracted from the model, i.e., the one given by the model's interpretation of the shapes and positions, and that such models exist. So the data types are captured relative to the interpretation of the sorts of shapes and positions, and absolutely whenever these sorts are fixed by auxiliary specifications, which we show for finite sets, products, dependent sums, and (co)inductive sorts built from them. We derive the induction, coinduction, and bisimulation principles as theorems, and illustrate the approach on lists and on Moore machines. This paper revises and substantially extends a paper published in EPTCS 389 (FROM 2023): several axioms are corrected, and the adequacy and satisfiability proofs are new.

papers.title: Canonical Proof Nets for Intuitionistic Multiplicative Linear Logic
papers.abstract: We study the problem of finding canonical representations of proofs in the multiplicative fragment of intuitionistic linear logic with units. We show that, contrary to the classical case, it is possible to define a notion of proof nets for this fragment which is provided with a polynomial-time sequentialization procedure and is both canonical and efficient. In particular, we show that sequent calculus derivations differing only by a permutation of independent rule applications are translated to the same proof net, and that the translations between sequent calculus and proof nets are inverse to each other.

papers.title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Quantized neural networks achieve computational efficiency by reducing precision, but bounding their quantization error remains a challenge due to discrete rounding and clamping operations. We present a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward network verification, introducing a unified round-clamp abstract transformer that jointly handles both operations. We extend this framework to constrained zonotopes, which add linear constraints to tighten bounds, and derive sound quantization error representations. We establish soundness and affine-strip optimality of the round-clamp abstract transformer, as well as convex-hull optimality of its complete constrained formulation. On the ACAS Xu benchmarks, our constrained zonotope method reduces average error-bound widths by approximately 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation at the two smallest tested perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6). These improvements are not uniform across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA achieves tighter bounds at larger radii. Our plain zonotope method delivers competitive sound bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.

papers.title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
papers.abstract: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $\mu$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.

papers.title: Proof-Relevant Interpolation for Circular Proofs in Linear Logic
papers.abstract: First introduced for proving Craig's interpolation theorem, Maehara's method provides a constructive, proof-theoretic procedure for extracting interpolants in sequent calculus proofs. Building on this method, Saurin developed a ``proof-relevant'' interpolation theorem for first-order linear logic, in the sense that the interpolated proof is obtained by cut-introduction steps that can be reversed via cut-elimination. In this work, we extend Saurin's proof-relevant interpolation to linear logic proofs with cuts as well as to circular proofs in linear logic with fixed-points. We specifically show how Maehara's method can be extended in a proof-relevant way to work on non-cut-free and non-well-founded (but regular) proof objects, and guarantee that the interpolation procedure preserves strong validity. We also study conditions under which one can interpolate system L terms that are not necessarily in normal form.

papers.title: CIRT: Calculus of Inductive Refinement Types
papers.abstract: Refinement types are a powerful mechanism for statically verifying properties of programs. They have been successfully integrated into practical languages such as Haskell, Scala, and Rust. However, their metatheory is not yet fully understood. In this paper we present the first semantic model for a refinement type system that supports the full feature combination of subtyping, SMT-style equality, impredicative polymorphism, and (stratified) inductive types. Interactions between these features have led to inconsistencies in the past, and existing formalizations of refinement type systems omit at least one of them. We present a realizability model based on partial equivalence relations (PERs) over a Scott domain, which overcomes these obstacles. We use our model to prove the consistency of a core refinement type system and to give a semantic account of the annotation-independence property of refinement types. Our semantics uses two interpretations: a refined one, which interprets types and their refinements as PERs; and an unrefined one, consisting of complete uniform PERs with a bottom element (CUPERs), which models computational behaviour independently of refinements. We extend the model to positive and stratified inductive types, showing that both are consistent in the presence of impredicativity.

papers.title: Base-extension Semantics for Intuitionistic Predicate Logic
papers.abstract: Sandqvist's base-extension semantics explains the logical constants of intuitionistic propositional logic by inference in bases: collections of rules over atomic sentences that record the inferential content of a state of affairs. We extend it to intuitionistic predicate logic, first- and second-order, reading the quantifiers substitutionally, and prove natural deduction sound and complete. Two ideas carry the extension. First, a rule of a base may require a premiss to be established for a fresh name, one about which neither the assumptions nor the base say anything. With such rules, Sandqvist's completeness proof extends to first-order logic, whether validity is taken over all bases or over finite ones. Second, the second-order quantifier ranges over the atomic predicates, and validity is support in comprehensive bases, where every expressible condition has a definitional proxy. This yields intuitionistic Henkin second-order logic with full comprehension, not full second-order semantics.

papers.title: A Direct Translation from Abstract Cyclic Proofs to Inductive Proofs
papers.abstract: We identify the notion of a `well-organized' cyclic proof, show that any cyclic proof can be unfolded to a well-organized one, and present a constructive and relatively simple translation from well-organized cyclic proofs to ordinary well-founded proofs. We work with a general class of cyclic proof systems, and translate from such a system to an induced inductive proof system: a multi-sorted predicate logic that extends the cyclic system with a well-founded induction principle. This setting is broad enough to cover trace-based cyclic proofs and size-change terminating functions. Our unfolding technique is a refinement of earlier annotation-based approaches, and allows us to handle cyclic proofs where the underlying inductive sorts need not be linearly ordered.

papers.title: Compact SAT and MaxSAT Encodings for Business-to-Business Meeting Scheduling with Idle-Time Balancing
papers.abstract: Business-to-business meeting scheduling assigns pairwise meetings to slots and locations under availability, capacity, conflict, and precedence constraints. The published Boolean formulation retains removable assignments and uses pairwise precedence clauses. We combine solution-preserving domain filtering, sparse shared-suffix precedence encoding, and an objective minimizing the range of participants' internal idle-slot totals. Experiments on 126 official and 100 higher-density derived instances separate domain filtering, precedence representation, transitive relations, and optimization method. Under the same objective, the compact model achieves median paired reductions of 40.3% in clauses and 55.9% in peak memory relative to an adapted published MaxSAT formulation. Domain filtering alone reduces assignment variables by 24.1% and clauses by 16.2%. Suffix sharing gives an additional clause reduction of 0.5%-1.0% on official precedence instances, reaching 5.5% at the highest density in derived instances that retain a known feasible schedule. Total-time changes are small and mixed. Internal idle distinguishes short interruptions from longer waits; aggregate idle complements the range. In the original one-run comparison, all three SAT and MaxSAT methods solve every official instance with lower median total times than Gurobi.
